network.description: A prebiotically plausible, nonenzymatic synthesis of arginine based on cyanosulfidic chemistry. The pathway begins with acetylene, hydrogen cyanide, ammonia, cyanamide, water, and hydrogen sulfide. UV-driven reactions produce an arginine aminonitrile precursor, which can theoretically undergo hydrolysis to yield arginine.
network.stereochemistry: The pathway does not establish enantioselectivity. The expected product is racemic DL-arginine rather than specifically L-arginine.

molecules.role: Prebiotic starting material and carbon-nitrogen donor
Prebiotic reducing agent and sulfur donor
Cyclized form of the guanidino aldehyde
Transient aldehyde for final Strecker reaction

reactions.name: Formation of acrylonitrile
reactions.conditions: Aqueous chloride-containing environment with Cu(I) catalyst
reactions.description: Acetylene reacts with hydrogen cyanide to form acrylonitrile, establishing a three-carbon framework.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition
reactions.description: Ammonia adds across the double bond of acrylonitrile, generating 3-aminopropanenitrile.

reactions.name: Guanidination with cyanamide
reactions.description: The terminal amino group reacts with cyanamide, introducing the guanidino functionality characteristic of arginine.

reactions.name: Photoreductive formation of cyclic guanidino hemiaminal
reactions.description: The nitrile group is photoreduced to an aldehyde. Intramolecular addition generates a cyclic hemiaminal, which is the observed form of the guanidino aldehyde.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally demonstrated transformation; formal coproduct balance shown

reactions.name: First cyanohydrin formation
reactions.reaction_type: Cyanohydrin formation with hemiaminal ring opening
reactions.description: HCN traps the aldehyde accessible through ring opening, producing a cyanohydrin and extending the carbon skeleton.

reactions.name: Conversion of nitrile into alpha-hydroxythioamide
reactions.description: Hydrogen sulfide converts the nitrile functionality of the cyanohydrin into a thioamide, retaining the adjacent hydroxyl group.

reactions.name: Photochemical deoxygenation
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation in hydrogen sulfide-containing aqueous solution
reactions.description: Photochemistry removes the alpha-hydroxyl group, producing the corresponding saturated thioamide. The coproducts represent formal net atom balancing.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of thioamide to aldehyde
reactions.conditions: UV irradiation and hydrogen sulfide-mediated photochemistry; formal net equation
reactions.description: Further photoreduction generates a transient aldehyde. The aldehyde is subsequently trapped with HCN rather than isolated.
reactions.evidence: Inferred transient intermediate in an experimentally demonstrated reaction sequence

reactions.name: Second cyanohydrin formation
reactions.description: HCN reacts with the transient aldehyde, creating the cyanohydrin with the complete six-carbon arginine framework.
reactions.evidence: Experimentally demonstrated as part of the photoreduction and cyanide-trapping sequence

reactions.name: Formation of arginine aminonitrile
reactions.reaction_type: Ammonolysis of cyanohydrin; Strecker intermediate formation
reactions.description: The cyanohydrin is transformed into an alpha-aminonitrile. This product possesses the complete molecular skeleton of arginine.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis to arginine
reactions.conditions: Aqueous hydrolysis under suitable acidic or basic conditions, potentially assisted by heating
reactions.description: Hydrolysis converts the alpha-aminonitrile group to an alpha-amino carboxylic acid, yielding arginine.
reactions.evidence: Chemically plausible extension using established Strecker hydrolysis chemistry; not demonstrated as the final step in the cited 2015 experimental pathway

prebiotic_environment.setting: Shallow aqueous environments, evaporative basins, or impact-associated geochemical settings on early Earth

scientific_confidence.overall: Plausible, partially experimentally validated prebiotic pathway
scientific_confidence.important_limitation: The cited cyanosulfidic experiments support formation of an arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor, not a demonstrated end-to-end synthesis of free arginine under one continuous set of early-Earth conditions.
additional_limitations: The formation and availability of all reactants in one natural environment are uncertain.
Some transformations require sequential changes in reaction conditions.
The final nitrile hydrolysis may compete with other chemical transformations.
The reaction sequence does not explain biological L-arginine homochirality.
Several coproduct equations are formal atom-balanced representations of more complicated photochemical transformations.

references.relevance: Primary experimental foundation for the acrylonitrile-to-arginine-aminonitrile reaction network.
